Front matter: title, abstract, keywords: A Latch-On-Resistant, False-Alarm-Gated Lead-Time Metric for Bearing Anomaly Detection — and What It Reveals About SCADA-Rate Logging Ansh Goyal1 1 Jaypee Institute of Information Technology, Noida, India anshgoyal500@gmail.com ABSTRACT Anomaly detectors for rolling-element-bearing prognostics are typically evaluated by classiﬁcation accuracy, which answers whether a fault is detected but not how early or at what false-alarm cost. We argue that lead time, the warning interval before failure, is the operationally decisive quantity, and we make it the primary evaluation object through a latch-on-resistant, false-alarm-gated metric. Warning time is credited only when the pre-onset false-alarm rate lies within a stated budget τ , so a degenerate constant-on detector is provably scored invalid. We then ask whether the bin-averaged logging of a SCADA historian destroys detection lead time relative to simple decimation. Eleven detectors (four statistical process control (SPC) charts, Isolation Forest, three deep reconstruction autoencoders, a root-mean-square (RMS) trend baseline, and two one-class models) are assessed under a controlled sampling sweep across four inferential run-to-failure datasets: XJTU-SY (n = 10), FEMTO/PRONOSTIA (n = 6), University of Ferrara (n = 6), and NASA IMS (n = 3). On IMS the variance-sensitive charts show a positive median shift (3σ +15.1 h), but the direction is not consistent across the three runs and does not survive Holm correction across the N = 44 family (smallest adjusted p = 1.00). We state the crossdataset conclusion as a bounded equivalence rather than an accepted null: against a pre-speciﬁed ±1 h operational margin—the resolution at which the result is actionable, since a maintenance planner cannot act on sub-hour differences in warning time—the run-level aggregate-minus-decimate difference is equivalent to zero in all 33 dataset × detector cells on the three multi-bearing campaigns, while on IMS the intervals are too wide at n = 3 to decide in 9 of 11 cells and favour aggregation beyond the margin in the other 2, and the single-asset gas-turbine record of the Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC, n = 1) cannot be tested. No cell shows decimation superior beyond the margin; in the ﬁve cells whose interval lies wholly below zero, decimation leads by less than the margin, the widest such interval (3σ on FEMTO) reaching only −0.45 h. The campaigns that supply this statistical power are short-lived bearings, on which an effect of the magnitude IMS shows could not have appeared, so the cross-dataset null bounds the effect at the scale of minutes rather than hours. On the short-lived bearings tested, deep reconstruction models do not overtake the control charts at any training fraction in [0.20, 0.60]; whether a crossover exists on long-runway assets is left open. The full pipeline, detectors, and result tables are released at https:// github.com/Ansh-Goyal01/Scada-Leadtime-Benchmark. Keywords: bearing anomaly detection, lead-time metric, false-alarm gating, SCADA historian, prognostic horizon, statistical process control, conformal prediction
Introduction: Condition-based maintenance (CBM) and prognostics and health management (PHM) promise to replace ﬁxed-interval servicing with data-driven intervention, reducing both unplanned downtime and unnecessary maintenance (Jardine, Lin, & Banjevic, 2006; Lee et al., 2014; Lei et al., 2018). Rolling-element bearings are the most common failure mode in rotating machinery, and a large literature applies statistical control charts, classical machine learning, and deep models to detect incipient bearing faults from vibration (Randall & Antoni, 2011; Zhao et al., 2019). The economic case is well established: a warning delivered hours or days before a catastrophic seizure lets an operator schedule an orderly shutdown, order parts, and avoid secondary damage to shafts, housings, and couplings. Despite this, most published detectors are evaluated with classiﬁcation metrics—accuracy, precision/recall, and receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC– AUC). These answer “was the failure detected?” but not the question a maintenance planner actually asks: “how many hours of warning did we get, and how often did the system cry wolf?” A detector that warns 48 h ahead at a low nuisance-alarm rate is operationally distinct from one that ﬁres minutes before breakdown or one that alarms every day. The prognostics community has long advocated time-aware metrics (Saxena et al., 2008; Saxena, Celaya, Saha, Saha, & Goebel, 2010; Goebel, Saha, & Saxena, 2011), yet lead time is rarely the headline quantity in detector benchmarks, and ad hoc lead-time deﬁnitions are easy to game. In particular, any lead-time metric that does not pair warning time with a false-alarm constraint can be trivially maximized by a detector that simply alarms from the ﬁrst sample—a “latch-on” exploit that earns the full run length as lead time while being operationally useless. A second, eminently practical question motivates this study. Industrial Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) historians rarely store raw high-rate vibration; they store decimated or time-averaged summaries at a coarse logging interval (Tautz-Weinert & Watson, 2017)—seconds to minutes, rather than the tens of kilohertz at which accelerometers are sampled. The folklore concern is that this storage step destroys fault-relevant information: that bin-averaging the summary statistics a historian retains washes out the very excursions that signal an incipient spall, so that the act of long-term storage would blind any prognostic algorithm that consumes the historian. Whether this is actually true is an empirical question that, to our knowledge, has not been tested with a sound lead-time metric across multiple datasets. The answer matters: if averaging is harmless, operators can store compact, cheap, bin-averaged streams without sacriﬁcing warning time; if it is harmful, the implication is that prognostics-grade monitoring requires separate high-rate acquisition. This paper makes both questions precise and answers them. We state the arc explicitly: Problem. Detectors are ranked by classiﬁcation accuracy, which ignores how early a warning arrives and at what false-alarm cost; and it is unknown whether the coarse, bin-averaged logging of a SCADA historian destroys that warning time relative to plain decimation. Solution. We make lead time gated by a leakage-free falsealarm rate the primary metric—warning time counts only when the pre-onset false-alarm rate is within budget—so that the degenerate latch-on detector is provably scored invalid rather than winning. Method. Under this metric we run a controlled sampling sweep that holds window content and alarm persistence constant, applied to nine detectors (four SPC charts, Isolation Forest, three deep reconstruction autoencoders, and an RMS-trend baseline; Deep SVDD, a deep support vector data description model, additionally evaluated) across four inferential run-to-failure datasets—XJTU-SY (n = 10), FEMTO/PRONOSTIA (n = 6), University of Ferrara (n = 6), and NASA IMS (n = 3), plus a real single-asset ONGC gas-turbine SCADA record analyzed as a case study (Appendix D.2)—with run-level signiﬁcance tests (the run, not the within-run sampling factor, is the unit of inference) and Holm correction. Finding. The folklore is refuted on every dataset tested: historian-style aggregation does not destroy lead time. On the large multi-bearing sets (XJTU-SY, FEMTO, Ferrara) the difference is negligible; on IMS the median shift is positive for most magnitude detectors but not consistent in direction across the three runs (not signiﬁcant at n = 3); the single-asset turbine record agrees (case study, Appendix D.2). The defensible cross-dataset conclusion is bounded non-destruction: no dataset × detector cell shows decimation superior beyond a ±1 h operational margin (the cells that favour decimation at all do so by less than that margin) (Section 6.4). Contributions. We make ﬁve contributions. 1. A latch-on–resistant, false-alarm-gated, onset-relative lead-time metric. Warning time is credited only when the false-alarm rate over a data-anchored, leakage-free pre-onset region is within a stated budget. We prove— by construction and by a unit test that is part of the released code—that a constant-on (latch-on) detector is scored invalid, while a detector that ﬁres just after the true degradation onset scores valid at zero false-alarm rate. We do not claim the metric is unconditionally ungameable; we discuss residual gaming surfaces in Section 8. 2. A formal proof that gating changes the answer. We give, to our knowledge, the ﬁrst formal comparison showing that an ungated prognostic-horizon metric (the Saxena PH) produces a different and operationally misleading detector recommendation relative to the false-alarm-budgeted metric (Section 6.11, Table 2): on IMS the seven detectors PH ranks highest by raw lead—the deep models, the one-class SVM, Hotelling T 2, Isolation Forest and the exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) chart—each have no valid operating point at a 10% false-alarm budget, whereas our metric identiﬁes 3σ, PH’s eighth, as the deployable choice. 3. A controlled SCADA-sampling methodology that holds window content and alarm persistence constant, so that any lead-time difference between the historian’s aggregate mechanism and simple decimation reﬂects genuine information loss rather than a window-counting artifact of coarser time grids. 4. A multi-dataset null result. Across XJTU-SY (n = 10), FEMTO/PRONOSTIA (n = 6), University of Ferrara (n = 6), and NASA IMS (n = 3), with bootstrap conﬁdence intervals and run-level signiﬁcance tests treating the run, not the within-run sampling factor, as the unit of inference, SCADA-rate aggregation does not destroy lead time, and on IMS shows a positive median shift for most control charts though not consistently across runs. No dataset × detector cell shows decimation superior beyond a ±1 h operational margin (the cells that favour decimation at all do so by less than that margin) (Section 6.4); nothing survives Holm correction across the N = 44 family. 5. Validation: wiring and empirical validation of a conformal detector for distribution-free false-alarm control, a lead-time–vs–false-alarm trade-off analysis, feature-group and spectral ablations that localize the prognostic signal to time-domain statistics on IMS, and a characterization of deep reconstruction models (an LSTM autoencoder, a temporal convolutional network autoencoder (TCN-AE), and a transformer anomaly detector) showing they do not become competitive with SPC charts within the tested training-fraction range [0.20, 0.60] on short-lived bearings; whether a crossover exists on long-runway assets remains open (Section 6.12). Scope of claims. The empirical results are for rollingelement bearings under approximately steady operating conditions; we make no claim of transfer to gearboxes, blades, or variable-speed machinery. The sampling question is speciﬁcally bin-averaged historian storage versus decimated storage. The metric itself is failure-mode-agnostic: it applies wherever a run-to-failure trajectory and a stationary normal region exist. We deliberately report a result that is not the one we set out to ﬁnd. Our working hypothesis was that bin-averaging the stored summary series would wash out incipient-fault excursions and shorten lead time. It does not. We regard reporting the refutation, with its dataset-dependent direction made explicit, as more valuable than a tidy but unsupported positive claim.
Prognostics, CBM, and Lead-Time Metrics: Reviews of machinery diagnostics and prognostics (Jardine et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2014; Lei et al., 2018) and of remaininguseful-life (RUL) estimation (Si, Wang, Hu, & Zhou, 2011) establish the CBM/PHM framing in which a health indicator is tracked and an alarm or RUL estimate is produced. Saxena et al. (2008), Saxena et al. (2010), and Goebel et al. (2011) propose a family of prognostic-performance metrics (prognostic horizon, α–λ accuracy, relative accuracy, and timeliness) that explicitly reward early, well-calibrated predictions. Our onset-relative lead time is in this spirit: it measures warning time relative to a degradation event rather than to an arbitrary positional marker. We depart from prior practice in one key respect: we make the false-alarm budget an integral part of the metric’s validity condition rather than a separately reported number, which is precisely what closes the latch-on loophole. We further provide, to our knowledge, the ﬁrst formal comparison showing that an ungated prognostic-horizon metric produces a different and operationally misleading detector ranking relative to a false-alarm-budgeted metric (Section 6.11, Table 2). The disagreement is not marginal: on IMS the seven detectors the prognostic horizon ranks highest by raw lead each have no valid operating point at a 10% falsealarm budget, while our metric identiﬁes 3σ, PH’s eighth, as the deployable choice. The cost asymmetry between a missed detection and a false alarm has been treated explicitly outside bearing prognostics. The Numenta Anomaly Benchmark (Lavin & Ahmad, 2015) scores streaming detectors under an application proﬁle that rewards early detection and penalises false positives, making the same commitment our gate makes in a different domain: that earliness cannot be assessed independently of nuisancealarm behaviour. The difference is structural. That benchmark folds both into a single weighted score, so a detector may trade false alarms against earliness and still rank well; our budget is a validity condition, and an alarm outside it earns no credit that a longer lead can offset. A parallel line of work revises evaluation itself for time-series detection. Tatbul, Lee, Zdonik, Alam, and Gottschlich (2018) generalise precision and recall from points to ranges with a tunable positional bias, so that early detection within an anomalous interval can be rewarded explicitly, and Wu and Keogh (2023) argue that widely used benchmarks admit trivial solutions and overstate progress. Our metric shares the diagnosis and differs in what it reports: rather than a score on a bounded scale, the gated lead time is a physical quantity— hours of warning—that a maintenance planner can act on directly, and the false-alarm constraint enters as a gate on validity rather than as a weight inside the score.
Anomaly Detectors and Control Charts: Univariate and multivariate statistical-process-control charts—the 3σ rule, the exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) (Roberts, 1959), and Hotelling’s T 2 (Hotelling, 1947)—remain workhorses of industrial monitoring (Montgomery, 2009) because they are interpretable and require little training data. In the unsupervised machinelearning family, Isolation Forest (Liu, Ting, & Zhou, 2008) and the one-class support vector machine (SVM) (Schölkopf, Platt, Shawe-Taylor, Smola, & Williamson, 2001) are widely deployed; deep models such as LSTM autoencoders (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997; Malhotra et al., 2016; Hundman, Constantinou, Laporte, Colwell, & Soderstrom, 2018) and Deep SVDD (Ruff et al., 2018) have been applied to machine-health monitoring (Zhao et al., 2019). We evaluate representatives of both the classical and learning families under a single, ﬁxed hyperparameter protocol so that the comparison is about the evaluation and the sampling question, not about detector tuning. Relation to published FEMTO/XJTU results. The FEMTO/PRONOSTIA and XJTU-SY campaigns are best known through the IEEE PHM 2012 challenge and subsequent remaining-useful-life (RUL) studies (Wang, Lei, Li, & Li, 2020; Nectoux et al., 2012), whose leading methods report a RUL-error score on the deliberately truncated Test/Validation copies of the bearings. Those numbers are not directly comparable to ours for two structural reasons: (i) they estimate a continuous RUL on runs with no observed failure, whereas our metric measures early-warning lead time on the complete run-to-failure trajectory and gates it on a pre-onset false-alarm budget; and (ii) they do not report a false-alarm rate at all, so a method’s RUL score says nothing about whether its alarm would survive our τ gate—the very quantity we argue is decisive. We therefore do not tabulate their RUL scores against our lead times, which would be a category error. The classic normalized-RMS health-indicator with a ﬁrst-prediction-time threshold—the workhorse baseline underlying most of that literature—is represented here by our rms_trend detector, evaluated under the same gated metric as every other method; re-evaluating speciﬁc published architectures under the gated metric (which requires their original code) is left as future work. The pairing of detection delay with a false-alarm constraint is the founding formulation of sequential change detection. Lorden (1971) posed the minimax problem of minimising worst-case detection delay subject to a lower bound on the average run length to false alarm, and Moustakides (1986) later showed that the cumulative sum (CUSUM) chart of Page (1954) is exactly optimal under that criterion; Pollak (1985) gives the corresponding result for a revised delay measure. Our gate inherits the same premise and applies it at a different stage: that theory constrains the false-alarm rate when a detector is designed, by choosing a threshold that meets a stated run-length bound, whereas we impose it when a detector is scored, against a rate measured on the data. The two can disagree. CUSUM, whose optimality theory this is, has no valid operating point on IMS at a 10% budget, because its pre-onset false-alarm rate sits at 19.0–19.8% across every threshold we sweep. 2.3. Uncertainty Quantiﬁcation and Conformal Prediction
Uncertainty Quantification and Conformal: Conformal prediction (Vovk, Gammerman, & Shafer, 2005; Laxhammar & Falkman, 2014) provides a distribution-free guarantee that the false-alarm rate is bounded by a target α under exchangeability. This is attractive for prognostics because it converts a detector’s raw score into an alarm with an interpretable, ﬁnite-sample false-alarm guarantee. We wire conformal calibration into the lead-time pipeline and, rather than assuming the guarantee, test it empirically across runs— including a run where exchangeability provably fails because the “normal” region already contains degradation.
Vibration Features: Bearing-defect frequencies, spectral kurtosis (Antoni, 2006), and envelope (demodulation) analysis (Randall & Antoni, 2011) are the classical frequency-domain tools for bearing diagnostics. We include fast Fourier transform (FFT) band energies, spectral kurtosis, and Hilbert-envelope amplitudes at the bearing characteristic frequencies, and we ablate them against pure time-domain statistics to see which family actually carries prognostic lead time under our gated metric.
SCADA-Based Condition Monitoring: Tautz-Weinert and Watson (2017) review SCADA-data condition monitoring and note explicitly that historian aggregation is a recognized but under-quantiﬁed concern: practitioners suspect that coarse averaging hurts fault detection, but the magnitude of the effect has not been measured with a principled warning-time metric. The present paper addresses exactly this gap, and reaches the perhaps surprising conclusion that, for bearing faults, the concern is not borne out.
Datasets: We use four inferential run-to-failure datasets spanning controlled-lab and cross-condition regimes, together with a single-asset real-historian case study (Table 1). They were chosen so that the central sampling claim is tested under genuinely different conditions: a high-rate rawwaveform rig where aggregation can be simulated faithfully (IMS), two multi-bearing campaigns (XJTU-SY and FEMTO/PRONOSTIA) that supply the statistical power a three-run rig cannot, a second modern constant-condition rig (Ferrara), and—as a case study only—a real historian stream that already is SCADA-rate data (ONGC, Appendix D.2). IMS. The NASA/IMS bearing dataset (Qiu, Lee, Lin, & Yu, 2006) provides raw 20.48 kHz accelerometer waveforms for three run-to-failure tests on a shaft loaded with four bearings. Because the waveforms are raw, frequency-domain features (spectral kurtosis, envelope) are meaningful; the coarsening sweep itself acts on the windowed feature vectors, not on the waveform (Section 4.8). IMS test 3’s failure label is set as documented in the released repository; the justiﬁcation appears in Appendix C. XJTU-SY. The XJTU-SY dataset (Wang et al., 2020) contributes ten run-to-failure bearings under two operating conditions (ﬁve bearings each) at 25.6 kHz, sampled in 1.28 s snapshots once per minute. With n = 10 it provides the strongest generalization test in this study; its published lifetimes range widely (52–533 min), which deliberately stresses the metric with both long-degrading and abrupt-failure bearings. FEMTO/PRONOSTIA. The FEMTO/PRONOSTIA platform (Nectoux et al., 2012) contributes an independent run-tofailure campaign: six Learning_set bearings under three operating conditions, with horizontal and vertical accelerometers sampled in 0.1 s snapshots at 25.6 kHz once every 10 s. We use only the six Learning_set bearings because they are run until the platform’s 20 g vibration stop—a failure, and hence a lead time, is actually observed—whereas the Test_set/Validation_set copies are deliberately truncated mid-life for the IEEE PHM 2012 RUL-prediction challenge and would make lead time undeﬁned. Lifetimes span ∼1.4–7.8 h. We deliberately exclude the Paderborn dataset (Lessmeier, Kimotho, Zimmer, & Sextro, 2016) from the lead-time study: it comprises pre-damaged bearings measured at ﬁxed operating conditions for fault classiﬁcation, with no degradation timeline and no failure event, so it cannot test a lead-time or sampling claim. Using it for the headline would be a category error, and we say so rather than pad the dataset count. University of Ferrara. The University of Ferrara dataset (Arpa, Gabrielli, & Battarra, 2024) contributes a fully independent run-to-failure campaign: six self-aligning double-row ball bearings under constant speed and radial load, with continuous uniaxial vibration recorded at 25.6 kHz throughout each bearing’s entire lifecycle (ﬁve-second snapshots, contiguous). Lifetimes span 0.7–6.8 h, similar to FEMTO. Operating conditions are ﬁxed, making the dataset directly compatible with our onset detector without normalization; we use all six available runs (E1–E6). The single accelerometer channel is duplicated into the two channel slots so the channel-invariant feature schema applies unchanged. The dataset is included to further test the non-destruction hypothesis with an independent 2024 rig; like FEMTO and XJTU-SY, its short bearing lifetimes mean this campaign cannot conﬁrm or deny the IMS positive trend. XJTU-SY (n = 10) is our primary inferential dataset; IMS (n = 3) is retained for its raw-waveform access, which permits the faithful aggregate/decimate simulation and the mechanism analysis (Appendix D.1).
Problem Formulation and Notation: For each run we observe a sequence of snapshots indexed by time t. A feature extractor maps each snapshot (and a short trailing window) to a vector xt ∈ Rd. A detector assigns a score st and, via a threshold and a persistence ﬁlter, an alarm indicator at ∈ {0, 1}. Each run has a failure time tf and is split at a train boundary tb; all scaling and threshold statistics are ﬁt on {t ≤ tb} only. The two quantities we care about are the lead time (how long before tf the ﬁrst sustained alarm ﬁres) and the pre-onset false-alarm rate (how often the detector alarms while the machine is still healthy). The remainder of this section makes each ingredient precise.
Channel-Invariant Feature Schema: Each snapshot yields per-channel time-domain statistics— RMS, kurtosis, skewness, peak-to-peak, crest factor, and variance—and, for raw-waveform datasets, frequencydomain features: FFT band energies, spectral kurtosis (Antoni, 2006), and Hilbert-envelope amplitudes at the bearing characteristic frequencies—ball pass frequency outer race (BPFO), ball pass frequency inner race (BPFI), ball spin frequency (BSF) and fundamental train frequency (FTF)—computed from the dataset geometry. A naive feature scheme that concatenates per-channel statistics and all cross-channel pairs is channel-count dependent and ill-posed: it produces 445 features for a 4-channel run and 1465 for an 8-channel run, against only ∼100 training snapshots, i.e. p ≫ n. Such a space overﬁts, is not comparable across runs with different channel counts, and silently inﬂates the apparent dimensionality. We therefore aggregate each statistic family across physical channels (taking the mean and the max over channels) and summarize each aggregated series over a rolling window with four descriptors (mean, standard deviation, max, and linear-trend slope), plus one cross-channel RMS-coherence feature. This yields a ﬁxed 49-dimensional space that is identical across 4and 8-channel assets and directly comparable across datasets. A train-ﬁt variance top-k selection (k ≤ 50) then guarantees p < n. All scaling is ﬁt on the training split only, so no test-region statistic leaks into the features.
Leakage-Free Degradation Onset: Lead-time metrics that reference an arbitrary positional marker (e.g. “the ﬁrst 5% of the test window is normal”) are gameable, because the marker is not tied to the physics of the run. We instead compute a single degradation onset to per run from a scalar health indicator h(t). The default indicator is the element-wise maximum of two baseline-standardized trends—the mean-RMS trend and the mean-kurtosis trend— so that it responds to whichever degradation mode (amplitude growth or impulsiveness) appears ﬁrst: ( ) h(t) = max zb[RMS](t), zb[kurt](t) , (1) where the baseline mean µb and standard deviation σb used in the z-score zb[·] are estimated only on data up to the train boundary tb, so to cannot see the test region. With band β = µb + kσb (default k = 4), the onset is the start of the last sustained excursion above β before failure, to = min{ t ∈ Rlast : h(t) > β }, (2) where Rlast is the ﬁnal run of consecutive above-band samples, merging gaps shorter than a tolerance and requiring a minimum persistence. Using the last sustained excursion makes the onset robust to early run-in transients and to the single trailing machine-off sample, both of which can otherwise spuriously mark an early onset. Algorithm 1 states the procedure. Algorithm 1 Leakage-free terminal degradation onset The terminal-excursion rule has a predictable bias. The onset ﬁres at the ﬁrst sample of the last sustained excursion above the band β = µb + kσb, so for a degradation ramp of slope m the estimator is late by approximately kσb/m, with a standard deviation of order σb/m. The persistence requirement P does not enter this bias: Algorithm 1 returns min Rlast, the start of the qualifying run, so P governs which excursions are admitted rather than delaying the timestamp reported for an admitted one. Both bias and spread scale inversely with the ramp slope: the estimator is near-unbiased and stable under abrupt degradation, where the delay falls to the sampling interval ∆t alone, and systematically late and more variable under gradual degradation. This accounts for the pattern in Table 3, where the abrupt ﬁrst IMS test agrees across all three health indicators at 98–99% of span while the slow-degrading second and third tests move substantially. The persistence (5 samples) and gap (10 samples) tolerances of Algorithm 1 are ﬁxed in samples of the health-indicator series, not physical time, and are held constant across datasets. The datasets are logged at different native intervals (∼10 min per snapshot for IMS after resampling to a uniform grid, 1 min for XJTU-SY, and 10 s for FEMTO and ONGC), so the same 5/10-sample bars correspond to ∼50/100 min on IMS, 5/10 min on XJTU, and 50/100 s on FEMTO/ONGC. This keeps the onset rule algorithmically identical everywhere at the price of exact physical-time comparability; the difference is negligible for long records but non-trivial for the shortest bearings: XJTU Bearing2_4 (42 min total life) must clear a ∼5-minute persistence bar, roughly 12% of its lifetime, so onset positions on the very shortest bearings carry this caveat. Caveat: onset positions on bearings with total lifetime below 2 h are treated as fragile throughout; per-bearing results in Tables 5 and 7 ﬂag these cases explicitly rather than silently discarding them. The sensitivity analyses probe the threshold multiplier k (Table 3), not these ﬁxed timing tolerances, which we leave in sample units for algorithmic reproducibility.

The lead time is ( ) L = max 0, tf − FAT hours, (3) 3600 with L = 0 if there is no alarm or if the alarm is at or after failure. The pre-onset false-alarm rate is the fraction of windows strictly before the onset that are ﬂagged, FARpre = |{t < to |{t : a(t) = < to}| 1}| , (4) measured over the entire apparently-normal region rather than a positional sample. An alarm is valid if and only if L > 0 ∧ FARpre ≤ τ, (5) with budget τ = 0.10 throughout. Where the pre-onset region is empty—the onset estimator places to at or before the ﬁrst scored window—FARpre is undeﬁned, so the alarm cannot be gated and is excluded from the validity denominator rather than counted as valid. Why the metric defeats the latch-on exploit. Reporting L and FARpre jointly, with the conjunction in Eq. (5), defeats the latch-on exploit. A detector that ﬁres from the ﬁrst sample earns a large L (the full run length) but ﬂoods the entire preonset region, giving FARpre ≈ 1 > τ and hence invalid. Conversely, a detector that ﬁrst ﬁres just after to has FARpre = 0 and a positive L, scoring valid. A unit test in the released code asserts exactly these two cases: a constant-on detector scores invalid, and an oracle that ﬁres at to+ scores valid at zero preonset FAR. Because to is computed only from training-region statistics (Eq. 2), neither L nor FARpre can be tuned using testregion information. We stress that this defeats the speciﬁc latch-on exploit; it is not a claim of unconditional ungameability (see Section 8).
Detectors: The headline set comprises nine detectors, evaluated under one ﬁxed hyperparameter protocol: • RMS-trend (naive baseline): alarm when the mean-RMS exceeds kσ above its training baseline. Included to verify that the metric penalizes a weak detector. • 3σ rule: alarm when the ℓ2-norm health index exceeds three training standard deviations. • EWMA (Roberts, 1959): an exponentially weighted moving-average control chart (λ = 0.2, k = 3.0), sensitive to small sustained shifts. • CUSUM (Page, 1954): a two-sided tabular cumulative sum (CUSUM) control chart (k = 0.5, h = 5.0) on the monitored magnitude—the classic change-point chart, most sensitive to a small sustained mean shift such as slow degradation onset. Deterministic. • Hotelling T 2 (Hotelling, 1947): computed in a principal component analysis (PCA)-reduced subspace (rank ≪ n) so the covariance is well-conditioned. • Isolation Forest (Liu et al., 2008): an unsupervised ensemble that isolates anomalies with few random splits. • Deep reconstruction baselines: an LSTM autoencoder (Malhotra et al., 2016), a Temporal Convolutional Network autoencoder (dilated causal convolutions), and a lightweight reconstruction Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017). Each is trained on normal feature-window sequences only and scores a window by its reconstruction error. Additionally evaluated (not in the headline nine). We also evaluate Deep SVDD (Ruff et al., 2018), a one-class deep model whose multi-layer perceptron (MLP) encoder maps normal data toward a ﬁxed center and scores a window by its squared distance to that center, and one-class SVM (Schölkopf et al., 2001). Deep SVDD produced no valid alarm on any FEMTO bearing at any training fraction below T = 0.60, and a valid alarm on exactly one of the six bearings at T = 0.60 (Section 6.12); it is omitted from the headline set; its full numbers are retained, unchanged, in the result tables throughout (Tables 2, 5, 6 and 9; Figure 6). We keep it visible because it is the low-false-alarm operating point under the gated metric (Section 6.9, Table 2). The deep sequence models carry a caveat: across bearings and training fractions these runs furnish between 20 and 335 normal training windows, with a median of 88 at the default split, so the models are data-starved. We include them to provide a modern-baseline comparison and to determine whether a ﬁnite commissioning-data requirement makes deep reconstruction models competitive with SPC charts, and if so to quantify it (Section 6.12). We do not tune them per-dataset, the same ﬁxed-protocol fairness applied to the SPC charts. On runs with fewer feature windows than the sequence length (short XJTU bearings, some coarse IMS factors) a sequence cannot be formed; we record that (run, detector) cell as an explicit N/A rather than dropping it silently. All non-conformal detectors alarm via a percentile threshold on training scores followed by a persistence ﬁlter, so the alarm semantics are identical across detectors and only the score differs.
Conformal Calibration: Figure 4a plots the empirical pre-onset false-alarm rate of the conformal Isolation Forest against the target α on each IMS run, with the exact values in its caption. The distributionfree guarantee FAR ≤ α holds on test 2 (0% through α = 0.10) and is essentially satisﬁed on test 3 (0.9% at α = 0.01, 4.4% at α = 0.05, so it holds through α = 0.05, while slightly exceeding the bound at α = 0.10, where the empirical FAR is 13%). The conformal machinery thus doubles as a per-asset usability test: it reports whether enough stationary normal data exists to control the false-alarm rate at all. FEMTO and ONGC calibration. The same per-asset usability test on FEMTO (Figure 4c) and the ONGC turbine (Figure 4d) conﬁrms the pattern and its limits. On FEMTO, no bearing honors the bound at α = 0.05 (empirical pre-onset FAR 0.08–0.56; pooled 0.27), because the short 1.4–7.8 h lifetimes leave a pre-onset region that is neither long nor stationary—the same reason the short XJTU bearings and IMS test 1 fail. The conformal guarantee is therefore usable where a stationary normal region exists (ONGC, the longer IMS/XJTU bearings) and self-reports as invalid where it does not (short FEMTO/XJTU bearings, abrupt onsets).
SCADA Sampling Sweep: We coarsen the time grid by a factor f ∈ {1, 2, 5, 10, 20} under two mechanisms: • aggregate: take the mean within each bin of width f , exactly as a SCADA historian stores a bin-averaged value; • decimate: keep every f -th sample and discard the rest. A naive sweep changes the window’s wall-clock span as f grows, which by itself alters lead time through a windowcounting artifact rather than information loss. Our controlled sweep holds window content and alarm persistence constant so that only the effective logging interval varies. This isolates the quantity of interest—does averaging lose fault-relevant information relative to decimation—from the confound.
At What Level Coarsening Is Applied: The aggregate and decimate operations are different experiments depending on the level at which they act, so we state that level for each dataset. On no dataset is the raw waveform coarsened: every loader reduces each snapshot to per-channel time-domain statistics at ingest, so the sweep operates on summary series throughout. On IMS the sweep coarsens the windowed feature vectors, after rolling-window summarisation, which holds window content and alarm persistence constant as the effective logging interval varies. On XJTU-SY, FEMTO/PRONOSTIA, University of Ferrara and ONGC the sweep coarsens the per-snapshot feature series: aggregate takes the mean of the summary statistics within each bin, and decimate retains every f -th snapshot. This is the operation a historian performs—historians store summary statistics, not waveforms—and it is the operation our claim concerns. It is not a test of raw-signal averaging. Averaging a raw waveform is a low-pass ﬁlter and does attenuate the impulsive transients that mark an incipient spall; we neither test nor dispute that, and Section 8 names it as the complementary study. The ONGC record is the clearest case, since its channels are the historian stream and no coarsening is simulated at all.
Statistical Protocol: Results are emitted in long format, one row per run × mode × factor × seed × method. Conﬁdence intervals are obtained by bootstrapping runs, which are the unit of generalization (resampling seeds would understate uncertainty). The run is the unit of inference. A single physical bearing run produces one degradation trajectory; the ﬁve coarsening factors we apply to that run (f ∈ {1, 2, 5, 10, 20}) are not independent observations but repeated transformations of the same trajectory—statistical pseudoreplicates. Pooling them as 3 × 5 = 15 “pairs” per detector (as an earlier version of this work did) inﬂates the effective sample size ﬁvefold and yields overconﬁdent p-values. We therefore collapse each run to a single difference, the mean of (aggregate − decimate) over factors, giving one observation per run: n = 3 on IMS, n = 10 on XJTU-SY, and n = 1 on ONGC (a single asset, for which we report descriptive differences only and draw no inference). On the resulting run-level differences we apply an exact two- sided sign test (binomial, H0 : P (aggregate > decimate) = 1 2 ). The sign test is assumption-light and the conservative choice at small n: it uses only the direction of each run’s dif- ference, making no normality or symmetry assumption that n = 3 could not support. A parametric mixed-effects model with three random-effect levels would be over-ﬁt and is de- liberately not used. Note that the test cannot reach signiﬁ- cance at n = 3: the most extreme outcome, all three runs concordant, gives p = 2( 1 2 )3 = 0.25. We report this ﬂoor explicitly so that the IMS direction is read as a trend, not a signiﬁcant effect. Runs whose mean (aggregate − deci- mate) difference is exactly zero after factor-collapsing are ex- cluded from the sign-test count; the n+ and n− tallies in Ta- ble 5 count only non-zero-difference runs. Across the detec- tor × dataset family of aggregate-vs-decimate tests (ONGC excluded, n = 1) we control the family-wise error rate with the Holm–Bonferroni step-down procedure at α = 0.05, stat- ing the family size N and the uncorrected FWER = 1 − (1 − α)N alongside. We use a single ﬁxed hyperparameter protocol throughout to avoid optimistic, per-condition tuning bias.
Experimental Setup: All experiments use a ﬁxed random-seed protocol; stochastic detectors (Isolation Forest, the conformal wrapper) inject the seed explicitly so that runs are bit-reproducible. The feature pipeline caches extracted features to Parquet so that the sampling sweep, ablations, calibration, and trade-off analyses all consume identical features. The released environment is pinned to the exact package versions that produced the numbers reported here, and a test suite (168 tests) asserts the metric’s ungameability properties, the leakage-free onset, and the conformal factory. The ﬁgures and tables in this paper are generated directly from the released result tables; no number in this manuscript is hand-edited.

Feature-Group Ablation: We ablate feature families on IMS for all six non-sequence detectors, reporting the valid-alarm fraction by group across the three runs (Table 10). The pattern is consistent and somewhat against expectation: time-domain amplitude features (rms_only or time_only) give each detector its highest or tied-highest validity, and admitting spectral, envelope, or the full feature set never improves validity for any of them. For the memory-based control charts it sharpens: rms_only is the unique group at which 3σ and EWMA reach full validity (1.00 at 0% pre-onset FAR), and spectral/envelope/all collapse all four SPC charts to 0.33 by driving their preonset FAR to 42–63%—the variance-sensitive charts react violently to the noisy extra dimensions. Deep SVDD is the instructive exception, and it fails for the opposite reason: its pre-onset FAR stays near 0% under every feature set (it rarely false-alarms), yet spectral features still cut its validity to 0.33 (and to 0.00 for spectral_only) by delaying or suppressing the alarm rather than inﬂating the FAR—the frequency-domain dimensions hurt the one-class deep model through missed detections, not false alarms. Either way the practical recommendation is detector-general on IMS: under a false-alarm budget, restrict every detector to time-domain amplitude features; frequency-domain features must be admitted with care, most of all for the SPC charts. Raw lead time inverts this ranking without overturning it: on Isolation Forest the envelope group yields the longest mean lead (99.4 h) and rms_only the shortest (32.0 h), but the long-lead groups accrue 23–29% pre-onset FAR against 0.2% for rms_only, so they buy their lead by ﬁring indiscriminately—and per run the same mechanism is visible directly, with spectral features ﬂipping 3σ, EWMA and Hotelling T 2 from valid to invalid on test 2 at 100% pre-onset FAR while Isolation Forest stays valid in both settings. Repeating the ablation at every coarsening factor leaves rms_only uniquely best at native and 2× resolution (f ≤ 2), matching the informational argument that bin-averaging preserves the amplitude statistic; at f ≥ 5 only a handful of windows survive per run, so valid fractions move in steps of 1/3 and whether the rms_only advantage holds at the coarsest SCADA rates is not resolvable at n = 3.
Comparison with the Saxena Prognostic Ho: If the false-alarm gate is what separates a usable warning from a manufactured one, then a metric without that gate should reward detectors our metric rejects. We test this against the most widely used ungated warning-time metric— the Saxena prognostic horizon (PH) (Saxena et al., 2008, 2010)—and show that on IMS it makes a different, and operationally wrong, detector recommendation. The PH is the interval between a detector’s ﬁrst alarm and failure, PH = max(0, (tf −FAT)/3600) hours, with no falsealarm constraint. It is exactly our lead time L before the validity gate (Eq. 5) is applied; that one missing conjunct is decisive. PH is maximized by the latch-on detector. A detector that alarms from the ﬁrst sample earns the entire record as prognostic horizon. On the three IMS runs this constant-on detector earns the full run length as prognostic horizon (164– 1073 h) while ﬂooding the pre-onset region (FARpre ≈ 1), so the gated metric scores it invalid on every run (L = 0); the oracle ﬁring just after t+o is the mirror image, at zero preonset false alarms and the maximum achievable lead (12.9, 62.5 and 44.5 h). Under PH the latch-on detector is the clear winner; under L it is scored worthless. PH and L disagree on the real ranking. The latch-on case is a worst-case existence proof; the more damaging point is that PH and L disagree on deployable detectors evaluated at their own best operating points. Table 2 ranks all eleven detectors on IMS by their best raw lead over the swept thresholds (PH) and by their best lead at an operating point within the τ = 10% budget (L). The two rankings are nearly inverted at the top. The seven detectors PH ranks highest—LSTMAE 199.6 h, TCN-AE 185.4 h, Transformer-AD 184.0 h, the one-class SVM 180.2 h, Hotelling T 2 176.9 h, Isolation Forest 174.7 h and EWMA 89.1 h—each have no valid operating point under a 10% false-alarm budget, so their gated lead is L = 0; the deep models alarm through 61–100% of every preonset region. The detector PH ranks only eighth, 3σ (77.0 h raw), is the one that actually clears the budget (56.3 h of lead at 8.9% pre-onset FAR) and is the correct recommendation; CUSUM (65.0 h, PH’s ninth) also scores L = 0, while Deep SVDD, ranked last by PH, rises to a valid 14.8 h. PH rewards precisely the detectors a false-alarm-budgeted operator must avoid. Implication. Any warning-time metric that does not gate on FARpre can be driven to its maximum by loosening the alarm threshold—in the limit, the constant-on detector. Our metric closes this by construction; the Saxena PH does not. The distinction is not theoretical: on IMS it changes the recommended detector from the ones PH ranks ﬁrst by raw lead to 3σ, the only classical chart with a valid operating point at a 10% budget. 6.12. Minimum Training Data for Deep Anomaly
Minimum Training Data for Deep Anomaly D: A practitioner commissioning condition monitoring at a new asset must decide how much normal run-in history to collect before a deep model can be trusted over a simple control chart. We quantify this on FEMTO—the one dataset where all six bearings are long enough for every detector, including the seq-len-30 deep models, to run on the full n = 6—by sweeping the training fraction T ∈ {0.20, . . . , 0.60} (calibration ﬁxed at 0.10, test = 1−T −0.10) with no per-T retuning. At T = 0.20 the shortest bearing (Bearing3_1) forms only 20 training windows, fewer than the 30 a sequence requires, so LSTM-AE, TCN-AE and Transformer-AD are recorded there as explicit N/A rather than as misses, following the convention of Section 4.5. Those are the only three N/A cells in the sweep; the remaining 297 of the 300 (detector, bearing, T ) cells are genuine evaluations. Valid-alarm fractions below are computed over the full n = 6 with an N/A counted as no valid alarm—the conservative choice—and the released sweep records the N/A count separately. The result (Figure 6) is unambiguous and, we think, more useful than a crossover point would have been: there is no crossover. The four SPC charts that deﬁne the baseline in Figure 6 (3σ, EWMA, CUSUM, Hotelling T 2) are already at or near their best at the smallest training fraction we tested—3σ at 1.00, EWMA and Hotelling T 2 at 0.667, CUSUM at 0.500—and more commissioning data does not improve them: 3σ falls from 1.00 at T = 0.20 to 0.833 at T = 0.30 and 0.667 from T = 0.40 onward, Hotelling T 2 falls from 0.667 to 0.500, EWMA is ﬂat at 0.667 throughout, and CUSUM is ﬂat at 0.500 apart from a one-bearing rise to 0.667 at T = 0.50. Isolation Forest starts from the same 0.667 and ends there too, but non-monotonically, dipping to 0.167 at T = 0.30 before recovering. Only the naive RMStrend baseline rises with T , and from a far lower base (0.000 to 0.500). This is a consequence of the design rather than a reverse data-hunger effect: the test fraction is 1 − T − 0.10, so the window in which a valid alarm can still ﬁre shrinks as T grows, and on bearings this short a larger training fraction buys a better-estimated baseline at the cost of a shorter opportunity to use it. The three deep reconstruction models sit far below the charts at every training fraction (LSTM-AE and Transformer-AD 0.000–0.333, TCN-AE 0.000–0.167) and do not close the gap as T grows: more commissioning data does not make them competitive in this regime. Deep SVDD produces no valid alarm at any training fraction below T = 0.60 and 0.167 at T = 0.60—one bearing, at the largest training fraction and therefore the shortest test window. The failure mode is the same as on IMS test 1: Deep SVDD ﬁres very late in the run, because its threshold requires substantial encoder-distance growth from the trained center before alarming, so on short FEMTO bearings (1.4–7.8 h) the ﬁrst alarm arrives after or coincident with failure on all six bearings at every training fraction below T = 0.60, and on ﬁve of the six at T = 0.60. This is a bearing-lifetime constraint, not a training-data constraint: the model is not data-starved in the usual sense but structurally unable to alarm early enough on runs this short. The practical recommendation is therefore narrower than “collect more data”, and narrower than a statement about the model class. On bearings of the lifetimes tested here, control charts should be preferred regardless of how much run-in history is available, because the deep reconstruction models do not overtake them anywhere in the [0.20, 0.60] training range. This is a statement about a data regime, not about the architectures: across bearings and training fractions these runs furnish between 20 and 335 normal training windows, whereas the models carry 2.0–5.5 × 104 parameters, so the comparison is made where the deep models are structurally disadvantaged. Whether a crossover appears on genuinely long-running assets, where a deep model could see orders of magnitude more normal windows than any bearing here provides, is the central open question. The closest publicly available single-bearing example is the KAIST bearing with a ∼43-hour lifecycle (n = 1, insufﬁcient for inference as noted in Section 8). Research groups with access to multi-run, long-runway industrial historian archives (gas turbines, compressors, paper machines) can apply the released pipeline directly; loader templates for all public dataset formats used in this study are included in the repository at https://github.com/Ansh-Goyal01/ Scada-Leadtime-Benchmark to minimize integration effort.
What Changed the Story: Four methodological corrections, applied together, change the conclusion of the sampling study. First, a correct failure label for the third IMS test (which had left a ﬁfth of the data after the nominal failure) turns a guaranteed miss into a valid detection. Second, an onset-gated metric that defeats the latch-on exploit prevents a constant-on detector from manufacturing lead time. Third, a p < n, channel-invariant feature space removes the ill-posedness of a channel-countdependent scheme. Fourth, a statistical test on the genuine unit of inference—the run, not the within-run sampling factor—replaces an eyeballed curve and a pseudoreplicated paired test. With all four in place, the original claim that SCADA averaging destroys lead time is refuted on every dataset tested, and the previously-reported signiﬁcant positive effect is corrected to a consistent but non-signiﬁcant trend.
Why the IMS Trend Appears but Is Neutral: The IMS trend has a clean candidate mechanism: binaveraging is a low-pass ﬁlter that removes single-window noise spikes, so the variance-sensitive control charts (3σ, EWMA) cross and hold their thresholds earlier under aggregation than under decimation, which keeps the spikes. This is consistent with the largest IMS median shift appearing in the 3σ chart (+15.1 h), although the shift is not consistent in direction across the three runs. The IMS trend is reproduced by an ordinary moving-average or Kalman ﬁlter on the decimated stream (Appendix D.1), indicating a generic lowpass-smoothing mechanism rather than historian averaging speciﬁcally. On ONGC the data is already smoothed at the 10 s historian rate, so further aggregation adds little; on XJTU the bearings are short-lived and many fail abruptly, so there is little quiet runway over which averaging could help. The synthesis is therefore not “averaging helps” but bounded non-destruction: across very different regimes, no dataset × detector cell shows decimation superior beyond a ±1 h operational margin (the cells that favour decimation at all do so by less than that margin) (Section 6.4), and where the signal is noisy and the runway long, aggregation shows a tendency to stabilize the health statistic. The single-asset turbine case study. The one real historian record in our study, an ONGC gas-turbine low-pressurecompressor bearing logged at a 10 s SCADA rate and ending in a genuine operator shutdown, has nine of its eleven detectors alarm 30–35 h ahead of the labeled failure (RMS-trend 22.8 h, and Deep SVDD not before failure at all), with an aggregate-vs-decimate difference of at most about a minute for every detector. Because it is a single asset (n = 1) we draw no inference from it and exclude it from the inferential family; we report it in full as a case study in Appendix D.2. It is nonetheless the cleanest illustration of the practical question, using no simulated coarsening, and is consistent with it.
Why Aggregation Preserves What Decimatio: Bin-averaging by a factor f is a length-f moving-average ﬁlter followed by downsampling: an anti-alias ﬁlter, then decimation. Plain decimation is the same downsampling with the ﬁlter omitted. The prognostic content of the health statistic evolves on the degradation timescale—hours—far below the post-coarsening Nyquist rate even at f = 20, while measurement noise in the same series is broadband. Decimation therefore folds out-of-band noise into the low-frequency band occupied by the degradation trend, raising the variance of the health statistic without changing its mean; aggregation attenuates that noise before downsampling. For a detector that alarms when the statistic crosses µb + kσb, a lower noise variance means the threshold is crossed earlier and held more persistently. The prediction that follows is about noise, not about detectors: the advantage of aggregation should grow as the noise ﬂoor rises. Appendix D.1 tests this directly (Table 15a), and the advantage rises monotonically as injected noise increases, from −0.35 h at the native noise level to +6.60 h at 10 dB, and is recovered by applying an ordinary moving-average or Kalman ﬁlter to the decimated stream (Table 15b). The feature space degrades unevenly under aggregation, for a structural reason. Each channel-aggregated series is summarised over the rolling window by its mean, standard deviation, maximum and linear-trend slope. The mean and the slope are linear functionals of the underlying series, so block-averaging them commutes with the summary up to the weighting induced by the 50% window overlap; the standard deviation, the maximum and the cross-channel coherence are not linear, and block-averaging them is not equivalent to computing the summary on the coarsened series. Aggregation therefore preserves the amplitude and trend descriptors more faithfully than the dispersion and extremal ones. We claim no conservation result. The detectors monitor a scalar collapse of the full standardised feature vector rather than any individual statistic, and the window overlap makes even the linear summaries a non-uniformly weighted average over each block. The argument states which descriptors degrade gracefully under aggregation and why the effect should track the noise ﬂoor; it does not predict the magnitude of the effect for any particular detector.
Practical Implications: For practitioners the message is reassuring and actionable. Storing bin-averaged vibration at SCADA rates, the default behavior of most historians, does not inherently sacriﬁce bearing-fault warning time relative to keeping decimated raw samples, and may even improve it for control-chart detectors on noisy long-runway data. The conformal results add a usable, distribution-free false-alarm guarantee wherever the normal region is genuinely stationary, and the trade-off curve turns the gated metric into an operating-point selector for a stated false-alarm budget. The ablations caution that more features are not better under a false-alarm budget: time-domain amplitude and impulsiveness statistics carry the usable signal on IMS, and spectral features must be admitted with care. Operators whose cost structure penalizes false alarms heavily (for instance, process plants where each alarm triggers a mandatory manual inspection) have a complementary operating point available. Deep SVDD consistently stays within budget at ≤ 0.6% pre-onset FAR across the swept threshold levels on IMS (Table 9), achieving 14.8 h of advance warning with near-zero false alarms. Where 3σ maximizes warning time within the 10% budget, Deep SVDD minimizes nuisance alarms for operators requiring near-zero tolerance. Neither should be used on IMS test 1, which the conformal machinery ﬂags as uncalibrated (Figure 4a).
Limitations and Threats to Validity: We state the limits of the evidence plainly, grouped by the kind of validity each concern bears on. External validity (generalization). The IMS “aggregation helps” tendency is a positive-median but non-signiﬁcant trend, sign-consistent only for CUSUM and Hotelling T 2 (n = 3; Table 6) and does not replicate on the larger XJTU or FEMTO sets (Table 5)—on FEMTO the only sign-consistent detectors, LSTM-AE and Transformer-AD, are negative; we therefore claim only non-destruction as the cross-dataset headline, not a positive effect. ONGC is a single asset (n = 1), reported as a descriptive case study with no inference (Table 6). The datasets, while deliberately diverse, are all rolling-element bearings; we do not claim the result transfers to gearboxes, blades, or other failure modes without further testing. A structural asymmetry limits what the cross-dataset null can establish. The three campaigns that supply statistical power—XJTU-SY, FEMTO/PRONOSTIA and University of Ferrara—comprise bearings whose total lifetimes span roughly 0.7 to 8.9 h, so an aggregation effect of the magnitude observed on IMS (a run-level median of +15.1 h for the 3σ chart) could not have been observed on them even if it were present. The null on these campaigns therefore bounds the effect at the scale of minutes, which is what our equivalence margin reﬂects, rather than bounding it at the scale of the IMS result. Conversely, the only dataset whose runway is long enough to express such an effect has n = 3 and cannot reach signiﬁcance at any margin. We therefore claim non-destruction at short bearing lifetimes, where the evidence is strong, and consistency with—not demonstration of—non-destruction at the multi-week lifetimes typical of industrial assets. Residual gaming surfaces of the metric. We claim the metric defeats the speciﬁc latch-on (constant-on) exploit, not that it is unconditionally ungameable, and we name two surfaces we do not close. (a) A detector could in principle align its alarm threshold to ﬁre just after the onset time t+o ; because our onset is computed only from training-region statistics, this cannot use test-region information, but an adversary with knowledge of the onset rule could still tune toward it. (b) The onset health indicator shares its RMS/kurtosis basis with several of the detectors’ own features, so onset and detection are not fully independent—a circularity that could, in principle, favor detectors aligned to the onset statistic. We acknowledge both rather than claim to have eliminated them; closing them (e.g. an onset signal disjoint from the detector features) is future work. Construct validity (does the metric measure warning time?). The onset deﬁnition, although leakage-free and stable to its threshold multiplier across k ∈ {3, 4, 5} (Table 3), is not the ground-truth defect-initiation time, which is unobservable in these datasets. A late onset—as on IMS test 1, where degradation and failure are nearly coincident—inﬂates the pre-onset region, can mark a genuine early detection invalid, and breaks the conformal exchangeability assumption (Figure 4a). The per-bearing XJTU breakdown (Table 7) shows the same effect: bearings whose physics provides essentially no warning runway score zero valid alarms regardless of detector, which is correct behavior but means the valid-alarm fraction is partly a property of the bearings, not only of the methods. Internal validity (is the comparison fair?). We use a single ﬁxed hyperparameter protocol throughout to avoid optimistic per-condition tuning, and we expose threshold sensitivity through the full trade-off sweep (Table 9) rather than reporting a single hand-picked operating point. The controlled sampling sweep holds window content and persistence constant so that the aggregate-vs-decimate contrast isolates information loss; the few-windows regime at the largest coarsening factor is annotated rather than hidden. Stochastic detectors inject their seed explicitly so results are bit-reproducible. Statistical-conclusion validity. Conﬁdence intervals are wide on IMS (n = 3); we resample runs, the genuine unit of gen- eralization, rather than seeds, which would understate uncer- tainty. Crucially, the ﬁve sampling factors applied within a run are pseudoreplicates of one degradation trajectory, not in- dependent observations: an earlier pooled 15-pair Wilcoxon test treated them as independent and thereby overstated sig- niﬁcance. We collapse to one difference per run and apply an exact sign test, which at n = 3 cannot fall below p = 0.25; after Holm correction across the forty-four-test family nothing is signiﬁcant (Table 5). The IMS result is therefore a directional trend to be read together with the XJTU and FEMTO nulls, never as a signiﬁcant effect. A parametric mixed-effects model is not used: with three random-effect levels it would be over-ﬁt, and the assumption-light sign test is the defensible choice at this sample size. The minimum- dataset requirement follows directly from the test itself: the exact sign test we use cannot reach signiﬁcance until at least six runs are sign-concordant (2( 1 2 )6 = 0.031). The three IMS runs are thus at least a factor of two short of the sample size a signiﬁcance claim would require—the quantitative content of the “long-runway, many-bearing campaign” the future work calls for. Long-runway bearing datasets with multiple runs are rare in the public domain; the closest available singlebearing example is a KAIST bearing with a ∼43-hour lifecycle (n = 1, insufﬁcient for inference). Research groups with access to long-running industrial historian archives—gas turbines, compressors, paper machines—can directly apply our released pipeline to test this hypothesis; we provide loader templates for all public dataset formats used here to minimize integration effort. Limited external benchmarking. We do not benchmark the gated lead-time metric against the RUL-estimation literature. The comparison is not straightforward—RUL methods predict a remaining-life quantity and are scored by prediction error, whereas our metric scores when an alarm ﬁres against a false-alarm budget—but the consequence is that the metric’s behaviour relative to that body of work is untested, and readers coming from RUL benchmarking should treat the two as complementary rather than ranked. Future work. Two extensions would sharpen these conclusions most directly: run-to-failure campaigns on long-life bearings of the kind typical in industrial service, where the multi-week runway could express an aggregation effect that short laboratory bearings cannot; and a comparable effort on other bearing types and geometries, since the four inferential datasets used here are all rolling-element bearings under approximately steady speed and load, and the single real-asset record is one gas-turbine compressor bearing.
Conclusion: We presented a lead-time-centric evaluation protocol for bearing anomaly detection, one that defeats the latch-on exploit through an onset-gated, false-alarm-budgeted metric, and used it to test whether SCADA-rate logging destroys detection lead time. Across four inferential run-to-failure datasets (XJTU-SY n = 10, FEMTO/PRONOSTIA n = 6, University of Ferrara n = 6, and NASA IMS n = 3) together with a real single-asset turbine SCADA case study (Appendix D.2), coarse aggregation does not destroy lead time, and on IMS shows a positive median shift for most control charts that is not consistent across the three runs (not statistically signiﬁcant at n = 3, and not surviving multiple-comparison correction across the N = 44 family). No dataset × detector cell shows decimation superior beyond a ±1 h operational margin (the cells that favour decimation at all do so by less than that margin) (Section 6.4). That null is bounded by the scale of the evidence: the three campaigns supplying the statistical power comprise bearings of 0.7–8.9 h total life, on which an aggregation effect of the magnitude seen on IMS could not have been observed, so the cross-dataset result bounds the effect at the scale of minutes and the multi-week runway remains untested. On the short-lived bearings tested, the deep reconstruction models do not overtake the control charts at any training fraction in [0.20, 0.60]; whether a crossover exists on long-runway assets is left open. The contribution is a reproducible methodology and a counter-intuitive empirical result: nondestruction, not a guaranteed positive effect. Future work will learn the degradation onset jointly with the detector so that the metric’s anchor is independent of a hand-set health indicator (closing the circularity noted in Section 8), and extend the conformal guarantee to the non-exchangeable early-degradation regime in which it currently fails. We release the full harness, detectors, tests, and the exact tables and ﬁgures of this paper to support replication and extension.

Appendix B: The 49-Dimensional Invariant: Each snapshot’s raw waveform yields six per-channel timedomain statistics (Table 13). Each family is made channelcount-invariant by aggregating across the physical channels with the channel mean and the channel max, and each aggregated series is summarised over the rolling window (10 samples, 50% overlap) by its mean, standard deviation, maximum, and least-squares trend slope, giving 6 × 2 × 4 = 48 features; a cross-channel RMS-coherence feature (the mean pairwise Pearson correlation of the physical RMS channels within the window) brings the total to 49. A train-ﬁt variance top-k selection (k ≤ 50) keeps p < n, and every statistic is ﬁt on the training split only, so no test-region information leaks into the features. Feature naming and the exact construction are in the released code (Appendix A).
Appendix C: IMS Test-3 Relabeling Justif: A subtlety we correct here is the failure-label of the third test: an earlier label placed failure on 2004-04-08, leaving 21.5% of the recorded data after the nominal “failure”—impossible for a run-to-failure series—so under that label the third test is a guaranteed 100% miss for every detector. We relabel it to the last recorded sample (2004-04-18 02:42), at which the mean-RMS health indicator has ramped from its ﬂat baseline (∼0.068) to ∼0.228 before the ﬁnal machine-off reading— within the ﬂat normal-region baseline band at the old label, but well above the 4σ onset band at the corrected one. The relabeling therefore moves the third test in the direction of harder, not easier, detection: a previously guaranteed 100% miss becomes an evaluable run, and because the aggregatevs-decimate contrast is computed independently within each run, the relabeling cannot artiﬁcially inﬂate it. We present this as an author relabeling based on the health-indicator trajectory, not an independently veriﬁed ground truth: we are not aware of a published benchmark that corrects this label, so we do not claim it as a community-established correction. It is nonetheless not a tuning choice: it only affects the single hardest run, and it makes that run pass rather than improving any aggregate-vs-decimate contrast (the contrast is computed within each run). It is the labeling we use throughout. The relabeling made our own claim harder to support, not easier. Because a reader may reasonably ask whether the label was chosen for the result it produces, we re-ran the entire IMS sweep under the original 2004-04-08 label and report both arms side by side (Table 14). The decisive case is the 3σ chart. Under the original label the third test is a guaranteed miss, so its aggregate and decimate lead times are both zero and the run’s collapsed difference is exactly 0.00 h; Section 4.9’s zero-difference rule then excludes that run from the sign-test tally, leaving 3σ at two positive and zero negative runs. An earlier version of this work claimed that in no run does aggregation shorten the lead time of the magnitudemonitoring detectors. That claim would have been true under the original label. It is false only under the corrected one, where the third test contributes −1.00 h, and we have withdrawn it accordingly. The relabeling therefore moved the evidence against the paper’s own claim rather than in its favor, which is the opposite of what a result-motivated relabeling would do. The relabeling is also narrower than one might expect. Under the original label the third test is a guaranteed miss for six of the ten detectors, not for all ten: 3σ, CUSUM, EWMA, Isolation Forest, Deep SVDD, and RMS-trend all score L = 0 in both modes. The remaining four—Hotelling T 2, LSTM-AE, TCN-AE, and Transformer-AD—alarm early enough to precede even the earlier failure time, so they retain a positive lead in both modes and their third run survives the zero-difference exclusion. The effective sample size is detector-dependent, and neither label can reach signiﬁcance. Because the zero-difference exclusion operates per detector, the original label does not simply reduce IMS to n = 2. It leaves neff = 3 for the four detectors that still warn on the third test, drops it to neff = 2 for 3σ, CUSUM, EWMA and Isolation Forest, and to neff = 1 for Deep SVDD and RMS-trend. The exact two-sided sign test ﬂoors at p = 0.25, 0.50 and 1.00 at those three sample sizes respectively, so under the original label six of the ten detectors could not have reached α = 0.05 at any effect size whatsoever. The four that retain neff = 3 ﬂoor at p = 0.25, which is itself already above α. The same ﬂoor governs the corrected label, where every run is retained but n = 3 still bounds the attainable p at 0.25. No IMS detector therefore reaches signiﬁcance under either label, and the best attainable p is 0.25 in both arms (Hotelling T 2). What the label does not change is the direction: no median ﬂips sign between the two arms, with 3σ holding at +15.10 h and Hotelling T 2 at +1.17 h. The Holm verdict of Section 6 and the headline are untouched by the relabeling.
D.1 Generic Smoothing vs.\\ Historian Av: The IMS trend admits a clean candidate mechanism: binaveraging is a low-pass ﬁlter that suppresses single-window noise in the health statistic, letting the alarm threshold be crossed earlier and held more persistently than under decimation. If that is the mechanism, two predictions follow, and we test both directly on IMS (controlling window content at sampling factor 5 so only the smoothing differs). Prediction 1: the aggregate advantage should grow with noise. We add zero-mean Gaussian noise to the per-window health statistic at signal-to-noise ratios of 30, 20, and 10 dB and recompute the (aggregate − decimate) lead time. To avoid the pseudoreplication we corrected in the main analysis, we collapse the four magnitude-monitoring SPC charts to one mean difference per run and treat the run as the unit of inference (n = 3 per level). The mean advantage rises monotonically as noise increases (Table 15a): from −0.35 h at the native noise level to +6.6 h at 10 dB, and at the two highest noise levels all three runs share the positive sign. The lone large negative in the table, the −7.94 h native-noise entry, is IMS test 1—the abrupt near-coincident-onset run whose degradation begins only ∼12 h before failure, the same run that violates the conformal guarantee (Figure 4a) and is unwarnable under every feature set. This is the qualitative signature of a low-pass mechanism—the noisier the health signal, the more bin-averaging helps. At n = 3 this is a directional trend, not a signiﬁcant effect (the exact sign test ﬂoors at p = 0.25, and at 30 dB the per-run signs are mixed). It corroborates the proposed mechanism; it does not, and at this sample size cannot, establish it statistically. Prediction 2: any smoother on the decimated stream should recover the advantage. If the beneﬁt is generic smoothing rather than the historian’s averaging speciﬁcally, then applying an ordinary smoother to the decimated stream should match bin-averaging. We compare a median ﬁlter, a moving average, a constant-velocity Kalman ﬁlter, and a wavelet denoiser against raw aggregation and raw decimation (Table 15b). The moving average and Kalman ﬁlter recover essentially the full aggregate lead time (76.0 and 75.6 h vs. aggregation’s 75.6 h), while the median and wavelet ﬁlters fall slightly short. The effect is therefore generic smoothing of the health signal, not a property unique to historian bin-averaging—an operator who decimates and then lightly smooths recovers the same warning time. The linear smoothers (moving average, Kalman) recover the advantage but the wavelet denoiser does not, dropping to 6/12 valid alarms—below even raw decimation—because its soft-thresholding of detail coefﬁcients perturbs the pre-onset baseline enough to lift the pre-onset false-alarm rate past the budget. The lesson sharpens rather than breaks: smoothing that preserves the normal baseline recovers the lead time, while smoothing that distorts it can cost validity. The onealarm gap between raw decimation (8/12) and aggregation (7/12) at statistically indistinguishable lead times (76.0 vs. 75.6 h) is sampling noise at n = 12, not evidence that decimation is preferable; it restates the headline.
D.2 Single-Asset ONGC Case Study: The ONGC record is a real Solar-Turbine low-pressurecompressor (LPC) dataset: four vibration channels logged at a 10 s SCADA rate over ∼5 days (42,698 rows), ending in a genuine operator shutdown on 2023-11-13 09:46. This is authentic historian data with a real, documented event—the maintenance record conﬁrms the shutdown followed a rolling-element bearing fault on the LPC—and the data-derived degradation onset (2023-11-13 03:44) precedes the operator’s action by roughly six hours. ONGC is the only dataset that requires no simulated coarsening to be SCADA-rate: it is the historian. On genuine 10 s industrial SCADA data ending in a real operator shutdown, nine of the eleven detectors alarm 30–35 h before the labeled failure (seven within 34.9–35.3 h, CUSUM at 33.9 h and Hotelling T 2 at 30.4 h), the naive RMS-trend baseline gives 22.8 h, and Deep SVDD does not alarm before failure. More to the point of this paper, the aggregate-vsdecimate difference is at most about a minute for every detector (Table 6). Because ONGC is a single asset (n = 1), we treat it as a descriptive case study and draw no statistical inference from it. On data that is already a real historian stream, the choice of logging mechanism does not materially change warning time. This is the cleanest possible illustration of the practical question—it uses no simulated coarsening—and it is consistent with “averaging is not the enemy.” The conformal calibration on this stream (Figure 4d) tracks the diagonal closely, consistent with a mostly-stationary normal region.
